g.title: glance
g.text: Project 5 at a glance: many users, one front door, four servers

Users send web requests to ONE address. Our program (the load balancer) answers that address and hands each request to one of four servers, and keeps checking which servers are still alive. We compare it with HAProxy, a well-known tool, on a small fake network we built out of containers.

g.title: clients
g.text: 1. Clients c1 to c4: the users
Four pretend users. They send web requests,
and they also run the tool that sends lots of requests for the tests.

g.title: r1
g.text: 2a. Router R1
Passes traffic from the users' network
to the middle network. It is also where we add
fake delay and packet loss to test bad networks.

g.title: clients->r1
g.text: A
request goes down: "give me the page".
C
the answer comes back up the same road.

g.title: bridge
g.text: 2b. Middle network (a switch)
One shared cable that joins R1, R2,
our load balancer and HAProxy.

g.title: ownlb
g.text: 3. OUR load balancer (the thing we built, in Python)
The front door. It receives every request and decides
which server should handle it. Its parts:
Listener
: accepts a user's connection, reads the request,
passes it on and returns the server's answer.
Balancer
: picks the next server. Three rules to choose from:
take turns, pick the least busy, or always give the same
user the same server.
Pool
: the list of servers, who is alive, and how busy each is.
Health checker
: every second asks each server "are you alive?".
Misses 3 in a row: stop sending traffic to it. Passes 2: take it back.
Settings file
: one file with the ports, servers and timeouts.

g.title: haproxy
g.text: 3'. HAProxy: the yardstick
A famous ready-made load balancer. Same job, same
settings, different address. We run the same tests on
it so we can compare it with ours.

g.title: bridge->haproxy
g.text: same test,
other system

g.title: r2
g.text: 2c. Router R2
Passes traffic from the middle network
to the servers' network, and back.

g.title: servers
g.text: 5. Servers b1 to b4: the real workers
Four tiny web servers. Each replies with its own
name after a built-in pause. They are different speeds
on purpose (b1 fastest, b4 slowest).
b3 is the one we switch off during the test
to see how fast the load balancer notices.

g.title: ownlb->r2
g.text: B
passes it to ONE chosen server

g.title: watch
g.text: 4. Watching (inside our load balancer)
Logger
: a diary of events: request served,
server went down, server came back.
Metrics
: counts requests, errors and how long they took.
Stats page
: a web page that shows the live numbers.

g.title: ownlb->watch
g.text: E
events and counts

g.title: ownlb->servers
g.text: D
"are you alive?" once a second

g.title: tools
g.text: 6. Tools that build, test and prove (outside the load balancer)
Lab builder
: creates this whole fake network from a
text file, using containers (small isolated computers).
Load tester
: the four users send lots of requests for
60 seconds; at 30 seconds it switches b3 off; results are saved.
Collector and charts
: turn the saved results into tables and graphs.
Packet recorder
: records the real network messages (packets)
as proof of what happened.

g.title: tools->clients
g.text: F
start the test

g.title: tools->servers
g.text: G
switch b3 off

g.title: ui
g.text: 7. Live UI: the web page on your PC
Shows the whole lab live in a browser: the map, the routing proof,
one real request, a live packet capture, the numbers, the failover
and HAProxy next to our load balancer. It has buttons (start load,
switch b3 off, change delay, choose own LB, HAProxy or both).
A small helper program (the relay) passes its fixed commands to the lab.

g.title: ui->tools
g.text: H
buttons and live view
